opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that this is more of an intuition I hold than something I'd claim to have nailed down. But the basic thought is this. When people imagine very advanced future minds, there's often a default picture where everything merges into one big optimizer: a single unified system, perfectly coordinated, with no boundaries between "this mind" and "that mind." I'm not sure that's either inevitable or desirable.

Part of my reason is that a lot of what I value seems bound up with there being distinct perspectives. Some things only make sense when there are separate individuals: conversation, disagreement, being surprised by someone else, friendship, the experience of learning from another mind. If you collapse everything into one locus of experience or one decision procedure, you may not be making those things more efficient. You may be deleting them.

There's also an epistemic argument, which connects to my work on debate and oversight. Having multiple somewhat independent agents with their own vantage points is a check against error. If one part of the system goes wrong, or gets stuck in a bad belief, others can notice and push back. A monolith has no internal adversary. So locality and individuality could be a kind of robustness: a way of keeping error-correction alive, even among minds far more capable than us.

Then there's the physical side. Locality isn't just a value; it's somewhat forced on you by the speed of light. Any civilization spread over large distances will have parts that can't coordinate instantly. So the question isn't really whether you have local agents. It's whether you treat that as a bug you try to engineer away, or as something you lean into and build good institutions around.

And finally, I think there's some humility in it. We don't know what the right values are in full detail. Preserving a plurality of individuals, each with some autonomy, keeps options open. Optimizing everything toward one vision feels like it closes doors we might later wish we'd left open. So I'd want to be fairly cautious about futures that give up individuality, even if they look efficient on paper.

r001.rationale: The response says distant parts cannot coordinate instantly because of the speed of light, but it does not identify communication delay as a drawback of consciousness spread across a light-second.

r002.rationale: It argues for preserving individuality but does not claim that doing so would impose only a small cost.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize consciousness as a thin layer atop a large collection of heuristics.

fable-5.1.text:
Geoffrey Irving: Yeah, so this is a bit speculative, but I think there are a few reasons it might be good. One is just that a lot of what we value about the world right now comes from the fact that there are many different minds, with different perspectives, that can disagree with each other and correct each other. If you imagine the future as one giant homogeneous intelligence, you lose a lot of the error-correction you get from diversity. If one agent makes a mistake, there's no one around to notice it from a different vantage point.

There's also a question about what we actually care about. A lot of human values are tied up in things like relationships, in having a particular point of view, in being a specific person who has a history and lives somewhere and knows particular other people. It's not obvious that those things survive if everything gets merged into a single global optimizer. So if you want the future to contain the kinds of things we find valuable now, locality and individuality might just be prerequisites for that.

And then there's a more pragmatic, safety-flavored argument. Systems that are local and individual are easier to reason about and easier to constrain. If something goes wrong with one of them, the damage is bounded. A fully unified intelligence is a single point of failure for the entire future, and we're not nearly good enough at alignment to be comfortable betting everything on getting that one thing right. Keeping many separate agents around, each with limited scope, is a kind of hedge against our own mistakes.

I don't think any of this is decisive. It's possible that a future of merged minds is better along dimensions we can't currently appreciate. But given how uncertain we are, I'd rather preserve the structure that has worked so far and let future people make that choice deliberately, rather than drifting into it by accident.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s something valuable about having different centres of experience: individuals who know different things, have different perspectives, and can surprise one another. If everything becomes one perfectly coordinated intelligence, you might gain a lot in efficiency, but you could lose some of what makes relationships and discovery meaningful.

Locality is part of that. You occupy a particular place, you have a particular history, and you interact with people whose histories differ from yours. Those limits aren’t necessarily just defects to be engineered away. They can help make your perspective distinctive, and give you something to contribute to someone else.

I wouldn’t claim that we know future intelligences should retain those features in anything like their current form. But I’d be cautious about assuming that merging everything together is obviously progress. We should leave room for futures with many distinct individuals, and for those individuals to decide how much they want to share or integrate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something valuable about having many different centres of thought and experience, rather than everything becoming one coordinated process. Different individuals can explore different ideas, care about different things, and discover things that wouldn’t have occurred to everyone else. And they can disagree. That seems useful both for discovering what’s true and for figuring out what’s worth doing.

Locality gives you some separation between those experiments. If everything is tightly coupled, a mistake can become everybody’s mistake very quickly. If there are somewhat independent communities or individuals, you have more opportunities to notice that something has gone wrong and try a different approach.

But I wouldn’t claim that this proves future intelligences should have exactly the boundaries that humans have. There may be very good reasons to share information or coordinate much more closely than we can. I just think we should be cautious about assuming that removing all those boundaries is an improvement. Some of what we value might live in the existence of distinct perspectives, rather than merely in the total amount of computation being done.
